approachQuestion.prompt: An editor must transform string a into string b. Each operation inserts one character, deletes one character, or replaces one character, at unit cost. Return the minimum total cost; do not return the edit sequence. Examples: a="map", b="mop" → 1; a="ab", b="ba" → 2; a="", b="ink" → 3. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 0 ≤ a.length,b.length ≤ 1500; characters are lowercase English letters.
Strings are read-only, indexed in constant time. Swapping two characters is not an operation.

options.text: Use costs for pairs of prefix lengths. Initialize the empty-prefix row by insertion counts. For each character of a, compute a new row with deletion, insertion, and diagonal match/replacement candidates, initializing column zero by deletion count. Keep two rows of b.length+1 entries.
options.feedback: The last operation either removes the last character of the a prefix, inserts the last character of the b prefix, or aligns the two last characters. These exhaustive choices depend only on the preceding row and the current row to its left.

options.text: Use the same prefix-pair recurrence and empty-prefix base costs, but retain the entire table of all prefix pairs.
options.feedback: The recurrence gives the correct minimum for every input. Since no edit sequence is requested, retaining rows older than the preceding row adds removable storage.

options.text: Count mismatches at matching indices through the shorter length, then add the absolute length difference.
options.feedback: An insertion can shift many aligned positions at once. For a="abc", b="zabc", inserting z costs one, while this method counts three positional mismatches plus the length difference.

options.text: Use prefix costs but also allow exchanging two adjacent characters as one unit-cost operation.
options.feedback: This solves a different operation set. For a="ab", b="ba", it returns one for a swap, but the legal minimum is two.

feedback.reason: Define a sufficient two-prefix state and derive exhaustive last-operation transitions with empty-prefix boundaries.
details: Initialize empty-string costs. For every prefix pair, compare deletion, insertion, and matching or replacing the last characters. Store only the previous row and the row being built, swapping their references after each row.

Deletion, insertion, and final-character match/replacement cover all last operations. The current row depends on its left cell and the preceding row; storing both suffices when only distance is returned.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze two-row-edit-cost with m=a.length and n=b.length. Allocate two arrays of n+1 entries, initialize the first row, and compute all m rows and all n inner cells. Swap array references after each row; do not copy rows or substrings. No early exit is used. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Treat m,n as independent variable parameters and account for empty strings. Array entries hold word-sized integer costs.

Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.

feedback.reason: Compute prefix-pair costs with two rows in the fixed column orientation.
details: Initialization takes n+1 work, row base entries take m work, and the inner cells take mn work. These combine to (m+1)(n+1), including empty strings. Two arrays of n+1 entries are retained. The algorithm does not exchange string roles to choose the shorter dimension, so n controls storage even when m is zero.
“O(m+n+1) time, O(n+1) auxiliary space”: Each pair of nonempty prefix lengths is computed; adding lengths omits the grid of states.
“O((m+1)(n+1)) time, O((m+1)(n+1)) auxiliary space”: Only two rows survive, rather than the full table.
“O((m+1)(n+1)) time, O(min(m,n)+1) auxiliary space”: This fixed implementation always uses the length of b for its rows. Choosing the shorter string would require an additional change.
